The Senegal jack, Caranx senegallus, is a carangid predator distributed along the West African coast, from Senegal to Angola. Field studies examining early life history have concentrated on the pelagic larval phase, a critical period during which neonates have a wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. The age at birth, or time to eclosion from the pelagic egg, has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable water temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days], a duration consistent with that reported for the congeneric blue trevally, Caranx melampygus. The lecithotrophic prolarva then progresses through a yolk-sac stage, relying on endogenous reserves until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit the onset of exogenous feeding. This early transition is a key bottleneck for larval survival, and the observed duration aligns closely with the thermal regime typical of the species' tropical distribution.

Sexual maturation in the Senegal jack begins well before the species attains its impressive maximum dimensions. Estimates derived from length-frequency distributions and gonad histology indicate that puberty is reached at a total length of 21 centimeters [Lp = 21 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 133 grams [Wwp = approximately 133 grams]. This weight is modest relative to the ultimate wet weight recorded for large, reproductively senescent adults, which can exceed 14.8 kilograms [Wwi = 14.8 kilograms]. The transition from a rapidly growing immature juvenile to a mature individual involves substantial morphological transformation, including the ossification of fin rays and the acquisition of the characteristic scutes along the caudal peduncle. Comparisons with other carangids of comparable body plan suggest that the onset of gonadal recrudescence at this size allows the species to capitalize on the seasonal upwelling-driven productivity that characterizes its coastal habitat.

Reproductive output in the Senegal jack is substantial, reflecting an iteroparous strategy typical of large, fast-growing carangids. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of its spawning grounds, which average 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], females produce a high number of eggs. This maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 10,960 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10,960 eggs per day], representing the peak fecundity documented for this species. This fecundity is inferred from comparative data on the closely related Caranx melampygus, and it positions the Senegal jack among the most productive members of its genus within the eastern Atlantic shelf ecosystem, where spawning appears to be protracted across multiple months.

Growth trajectories for this species show a pronounced allometric relationship between length and mass. The ultimate total length recorded for the Senegal jack is 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a size that defines the upper limit of its size spectrum in coastal fisheries. This ultimate length corresponds to an asymptotic body mass of 14,800 grams [Wwi = 14,800 grams], calculated from a standard length-weight regression. The growth pattern is characterized by rapid early gains during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, followed by a gradual deceleration as individuals approach their maximum size. Longevity data from mark-recapture programs and otolith ageing indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when measured at the average ambient temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a fish of this ultimate length and suggests a life history strategy that balances relatively fast somatic growth with a protracted reproductive window, allowing multiple annual spawning cycles over the course of an adult's lifetime.

From a comparative and ecological perspective, the Senegal jack occupies a specialized niche as a pelagic predator in coastal and estuarine waters, feeding predominantly on small clupeids, cephalopods, and crustaceans. The life history traits described above—an elevated fecundity, a size at puberty of 21 centimeters [Lp = 21 centimeters], and a moderate maximum age of 10 years [am = 10 years]—collectively underscore a strategy adapted to variable, productivity-driven environments at a temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C]. The relatively brief yolk-sac larval phase, hatching after 7.5 days [ab = 7.5 days] at 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], ensures rapid transition to exogenous feeding and minimizes vulnerability to predation during the earliest life stages. In comparison to other exploited carangids in the region, such as the horse mackerel (Trachurus trachurus), the Senegal jack exhibits a more extended growth period and a higher ultimate body mass, traits that may confer competitive advantages in prey capture but also render it more susceptible to size-selective fishing pressure. These demographic parameters provide a basis for stock assessment models and for evaluating the species' resilience to environmental change.
